source_notes.finding: CodeModeExecutor.setup() passes env_vars=dict(os.environ) and DockerSandbox puts env_vars into the container environment. With the host's HOME=/Users/<user> inside the container, jupyter server crashes creating its runtime directory (PermissionError: [Errno 13] Permission denied: '/Users'), and setup ends with 'Timed out waiting for Jupyter Server'. Reproduced directly with docker run -e HOME=... on the same image.

The container starts, then register_tool_caller(self.call_tool) asks the kernel client to set_variable('__call_tool__', bound_method), which pickles it and fails: 'Cannot serialize variable __call_tool__ ... Can't get local object _make_handshake_stamp.<locals>.stamp'.
By design the default path ships the full host environment, secrets included, into the container (failure 1 shows it arrives). That would make P5 'works' even inside Docker if setup succeeded.

DockerSandbox starts the container on the default bridge network with a published Jupyter port and never reads network_policy, so outbound network would be on. The host port is chosen by Docker (ports={'8888/tcp': ('127.0.0.1', None)}), with no option to pin it.

For non-eval variants, tools are regenerated inside the kernel and called either through an HTTP proxy (mcp_proxy_url, served by the separate agent-runtimes project) or by MCP clients created inside the kernel from the host's server configs. The second needs agent_codemode installed in the image and the MCP server command runnable inside the container; neither is true for this image.

surprises: The documented docker variant cannot start through CodeModeExecutor on this Mac: forwarding the host environment into the container breaks Jupyter, and even with an empty environment the tool caller cannot be pickled into the kernel.
network_policy is a SandboxConfig field but DockerSandbox ignores it; the container gets normal outbound networking.
The container's host port is assigned by Docker and cannot be configured, so this probe could not keep to the 41500-41599 range (ports were ephemeral on 127.0.0.1).
